title: How to store and preserve comic books
answer: Keep comics cool, dry, dark and flat or upright with support: bag and board every raw book with acid-free materials, store them in archival boxes away from exterior walls, floors, sunlight and heat sources, and aim for a stable temperature around 18–21 °C and relative humidity around 40–50 %. Slabs need the same environment; the case protects against handling, not against heat, humidity or ultraviolet light.
body:
## The enemies of paper

- **Heat** speeds up the acid reactions that turn newsprint yellow and brittle.
- **Humidity** encourages mould, foxing and warping; very dry air makes paper brittle.
- **Light**, especially ultraviolet, fades inks and yellows paper.
- **Acid** migrates from cheap cardboard, wood and old bags into the book.
- **Pressure and handling** cause spine stress, bends and creases.

## Raw books

1. **Bag and board.** A polypropylene, polyethylene or Mylar bag with an acid-free, buffered backing board behind the book. See [Bags and boards](/guides/comic-bags-and-boards-explained).
2. **Box them upright** in an archival comic box, snug enough that the books do not lean but not so tight they are compressed. Use dividers to keep runs vertical.
3. **Replace bags** every few years; polypropylene and polyethylene yellow and off-gas with age. Mylar lasts decades.

## Slabs

Store them upright in a slab box or flat in shallow stacks, each in a bag to prevent scuffing. Do not stack more than a few high. Keep them out of direct sunlight; the case blocks some UV but not all, and it does nothing about heat.

## The room

- Interior room, not a garage, attic, basement or shed.
- Off the floor and away from exterior walls, windows, radiators and pipes.
- A cheap hygrometer tells you the humidity; a dehumidifier or a sealed container with silica gel controls it.
- Stable matters as much as ideal: swings in temperature and humidity do more harm than a steady 22 °C.

## Handling

Clean, dry hands; no food or drink; open a book flat rather than bending it back; never lick a finger to turn a page. Golden Age paper can be brittle — support the cover and centrefold when you open it.

## Insurance and records

Storage protects against damage; an inventory and insurance protect against loss. See [How to insure a comic collection](/guides/how-to-insure-a-comic-collection).

For books you do not need at home, our [vault storage](/services/vault-storage) keeps them in controlled conditions.

title: Comic bags and boards explained: sizes, materials and what to buy
answer: A bag protects a comic from dirt and handling; a board keeps it flat and, if it is acid-free and buffered, absorbs acid. Bags come in Golden, Silver, Current (Modern) and magazine sizes to match how comic dimensions have shrunk over the decades, and in three materials: polypropylene and polyethylene (cheap, replace every few years) and Mylar (polyester, archival, lasts decades). Buy the size that matches the book's era and use boards labelled acid-free.
body:
## Sizes

Comics got smaller over time, so bags and boards come in era sizes. Approximate widths:

| Size | Fits | Typical bag width |
|---|---|---|
| Golden Age | 1938 to mid-1950s | about 7¾ in (19.7 cm) |
| Silver Age | mid-1950s to about 1980 | about 7⅛ in (18.1 cm) |
| Current / Modern | 1980s to today | about 6⅞ in (17.5 cm) |
| Magazine | Oversized magazines and treasuries | wider formats |

The sizes overlap; a Silver Age bag fits most Bronze Age books comfortably, and many collectors use Silver size for everything from the 1960s to the 1980s. If a book is a tight fit, go up a size — forcing a comic into a bag causes spine stress.

## Materials

- **Polypropylene (PP)** — clear, cheap, the standard shop bag. Yellows and becomes brittle after some years; replace periodically.
- **Polyethylene (PE)** — softer and cloudier, cheap, similar lifespan.
- **Mylar (polyester, often sold as Mylites)** — crystal clear, inert, archival; lasts decades and does not off-gas. The right choice for keys and long-term storage; costs more.

## Boards

A backing board should be **acid-free**, and ideally **buffered** with calcium carbonate to neutralise acid migrating from the paper. Boards are sold in the same era sizes as bags. Put the board behind the book, glossy side towards the comic, and slide the pair into the bag with the opening at the top.

## Tape

Seal the bag flap with a small piece of tape onto the bag, not the board, and never onto the comic. When opening, cut the tape rather than peeling, which can pull the flap into the book.

## Slab bags

Graded slabs go in their own oversized bags to prevent scuffs on the case.

See [How to store and preserve comics](/guides/how-to-store-and-preserve-comics) for the rest of the storage picture.

title: How to ship a graded comic (CGC or CBCS slab) safely
answer: Put the slab in a bag, sandwich it between two pieces of rigid cardboard or foam larger than the case, wrap it in bubble wrap, and place it in a sturdy box with at least 5 cm (2 inches) of padding on every side so it cannot move. Ship with tracking and full-value insurance, require a signature for anything valuable, and never let the slab touch the outside walls of the box. The case protects the comic; the packaging has to protect the case.
body:
## What goes wrong

Slabs crack at the corners and along the seam when a box is dropped on its edge and the case is against the wall. Newton rings and shifted books happen when the case flexes. Every one of these is a padding failure.

## Step by step

1. **Bag the slab** to prevent scuffs.
2. **Sandwich it** between two rigid boards (corrugated cardboard, foam board or a purpose-made slab mailer) cut larger than the case. Tape the boards together around the edges so the slab cannot slide out.
3. **Wrap** the sandwich in two or three layers of bubble wrap.
4. **Box it** in a box at least 5 cm larger than the wrapped package on every side. Fill the gaps with bubble wrap, foam or crumpled paper so nothing moves when you shake the box.
5. **Seal** all seams with packing tape.
6. **Ship** with tracking and insurance for the full value. For high-value books, add a signature requirement and consider double-boxing (the packed box inside a second box with more padding).

## Multiple slabs

Stack slabs with a divider between each, then treat the stack as one item. Do not let cases rub against each other. Keep the total weight sensible; a heavy box gets dropped.

## Insurance

Carrier insurance has limits and exclusions for collectibles. For valuable books use the carrier's declared-value service if it covers comics, or third-party shipping insurance. Photograph the slab and the packed box before sealing.

## Labelling

Do not write "comics" or "collectibles" on the outside. "Fragile" does no harm.

## How we ship

Every slab sold on this marketplace ships in a rigid sandwich inside a padded box with tracking and insurance, and high-value orders require a signature. Details and rates are on the [shipping policy](/policies/shipping).

title: How to ship raw comics without damaging them
answer: Bag and board each comic, sandwich the stack between two pieces of rigid cardboard larger than the books, tape the sandwich so nothing can shift, and put it in a box or rigid mailer with padding so the sandwich cannot bend or move. Never ship a raw comic in a plain envelope, and never let the corners of the books reach the edge of the package. Use tracking, and insure anything worth more than the postage.
body:
## The rules

- **Rigid on both sides.** A single board lets the package fold around the book. Two boards, larger than the comic, taped together, is the minimum.
- **No movement.** A comic that slides inside its package gets corner damage and spine stress. Tape the sandwich; fill the box.
- **Corners away from edges.** The most vulnerable part of a comic is a corner; keep it at least a couple of centimetres from any edge of the package.
- **Water.** Put the sandwich in a polythene bag before boxing. Mail gets wet.

## Step by step

1. Bag and board each book.
2. Stack up to about ten books with boards between groups; more than that, split the shipment.
3. Cut two pieces of stiff corrugated cardboard slightly larger than the stack, with the flutes running in opposite directions for stiffness.
4. Tape the sandwich around all four edges.
5. Bag it, then box it with padding on every side, or use a rigid mailer sized so the sandwich fits without slack.
6. Tracking on everything; insurance on anything worth insuring.

## Golden Age and brittle books

Brittle paper cracks under flex. Add a third board and more padding, ship flat rather than upright, and avoid cold-weather shipping when possible — cold makes brittle paper worse.

## Sending books for grading

The grading companies publish packing instructions for submissions; they are essentially the method above. Our [grading submission service](/services/grading-submission) includes insured shipping both ways so you do not have to.

For slabs, see [How to ship a graded comic](/guides/how-to-ship-a-graded-comic).

title: How do I clean a CGC or CBCS slab?
answer: Wipe the outside of the case with a soft microfibre cloth, dry or very slightly dampened with water. For stubborn marks, a small amount of plastic-safe cleaner on the cloth, not on the case. Never use solvents, alcohol, ammonia-based glass cleaner or abrasive pads, which cloud the acrylic, and never let liquid reach the seam or the label window. Scratches cannot be polished out safely; a badly scuffed case is a reholder job.
body:
## Routine cleaning

1. Blow or brush off dust so you are not dragging grit across the plastic.
2. Wipe gently with a clean microfibre cloth. Most fingerprints come off dry.
3. For greasy marks, breathe on the case or barely dampen the cloth with water, wipe, then dry with a second cloth.

## What not to use

- **Alcohol, acetone, ammonia (most glass cleaners)** — they craze and cloud acrylic.
- **Paper towels and tissues** — they leave fine scratches.
- **Abrasive polishes**, including many "plastic polishes", unless specifically rated for acrylic and tested on a corner first.
- **Soaking** — liquid at the seam or under the label window can reach the book.

## Scratches and scuffs

Light surface scuffs sometimes soften with an acrylic-safe polish, but the risk of making a hazy patch is real. If the case detracts from display or sale, the grader's reholder service replaces it and the grade is unchanged. See [What are Newton rings?](/guides/what-are-newton-rings) for the other common cosmetic complaint.

## Prevention

Keep slabs in bags; scuffs come from cases rubbing on each other and on shelves. Handle by the edges, and keep them out of sunlight, which yellows older plastics over time.

title: What temperature and humidity should comics be stored at?
answer: Cool, dry and stable: a temperature around 18–21 °C (65–70 °F) and relative humidity around 40–50 %, with as little daily swing as possible. Below about 35 % paper becomes brittle; above about 55–60 % mould and foxing become a risk. Heat is the accelerator for every kind of paper decay, so a stable 20 °C beats a room that cycles between 15 °C and 28 °C.
body:
## The targets

| Measure | Aim for | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Temperature | 18–21 °C, stable | Over 24 °C, and daily swings |
| Relative humidity | 40–50 % | Under 35 % or over 55 % |
| Light | Dark | Direct sun and unfiltered fluorescent light |

These are the ranges archives and libraries use for paper; comic paper is cheaper than most, so if anything it needs them more.

## Why each matters

- **Heat** roughly doubles the rate of chemical decay for every 10 °C rise. The difference between an attic and a cool interior room, over decades, is the difference between white and tan pages.
- **High humidity** feeds mould, causes the brown spots called foxing, and lets the paper absorb water and ripple.
- **Low humidity** dries the paper and makes it brittle — particularly dangerous for Golden Age newsprint.
- **Swings** make paper expand and contract, loosening staples and stressing spines.

## Measuring and controlling

- A digital hygrometer with a min/max memory shows what the room actually does across a day and a season.
- A small dehumidifier or a sealed container with silica gel brings humidity down; a humidifier or a simple bowl of water in the cupboard brings it up in dry winters.
- Interior rooms and closets are naturally more stable than rooms with exterior walls.

## Slabs are not sealed environments

A grading holder is not airtight. The book inside breathes with the room. MicroChamber paper inserted by the grader slows decay but does not replace a good environment.

See [How to store and preserve comics](/guides/how-to-store-and-preserve-comics) for the rest.

title: How to display graded comics without damaging them
answer: Display slabs out of direct sunlight and away from heat, in stands or frames that support the case without pressure on it, and rotate what is on display so no single book spends years under light. Use UV-filtering acrylic or glass in front of anything on a wall. The case does not stop ultraviolet light from fading the cover, and a shelf above a radiator or in a sunny window will do more harm in a year than decades of box storage.
body:
## Light

Fading is cumulative and irreversible. Rules:

- No direct sunlight, ever.
- Prefer LED lighting, which emits almost no UV, over halogen or fluorescent.
- For wall frames, use UV-filtering acrylic and hang on an interior wall.
- Rotate: a month on display and a year in the box preserves the colour of every book you own.

## Heat

Not above a radiator, fireplace, television or amplifier. Not in a conservatory. Heat cycles are worse than steady warmth.

## Physical support

- Acrylic slab stands and frames sold for graded comics hold the case by its edges without clamps.
- Do not lean slabs against each other or rest them on a corner.
- Wall frames should support the weight from below; never hang a case by a hook through it.

## Security

A display is an advertisement. Keep the most valuable books in storage and display good-looking mid-grade copies, or copies of books whose value is modest. Photograph what is on display for insurance.

## Raw books

Raw books should not be displayed long-term; the cover fades and the spine sags. A framed, bagged and boarded copy behind UV acrylic is acceptable for a reading copy.

See [How to store and preserve comics](/guides/how-to-store-and-preserve-comics) and [Temperature and humidity for comics](/guides/temperature-and-humidity-for-comics).
